title: Addressing Modes and Memory Access
subtitle: How an instruction finds its operands and its targets.

references.title: Instructions: Language of the Computer
references.topics: MIPS addressing for branches and jumps; memory operands; byte and half-word loads and stores; byte order and alignment

objectives: Name the MIPS addressing modes and say where each finds its operand
Calculate effective addresses for lw and sw (base plus displacement)
Calculate branch and jump targets (PC-relative and pseudo-direct)
Explain alignment and what happens when it is violated
Compare big endian and little endian byte order

steps.question: A program can use over four billion addresses, but `lw` has only 16 bits for an offset. How can it still reach any element of any array?
clues: An address is a 32-bit number; the offset field is only 16 bits.
The trick: add a small offset to a **base address** kept in a register.
Ways of finding an operand or a target are called **addressing modes**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Where does an operand come from?

head: Mode
Where the operand or target is
MIPS example
rows: Target built from the jump field and the PC

steps.why: Each mode is a different way of turning bits in the instruction into a value or an address. The ISA picks a few good ones.
steps.real: Every array access, loop and function call you write uses one of these modes.

explainAgain.beginner: An addressing mode is just the rule for finding the thing the instruction works on.

notes.explain: Reveal rows one at a time. Students already met immediate, register and base+offset in Class 5.

stages.label: Operands

stages.label: Operands
stages.text: Both are read from the register file

steps.why: No memory access is needed in either mode, so these are the fastest.

steps.question: Which addressing mode do the operands of `add $t0, $s1, $s2` use?
steps.why: All three operands are registers.
feedback: An immediate would be a constant written in the instruction.

steps.prompt: Match each instruction with its addressing mode.
steps.why: The operand fields tell you the mode.

steps.title: Base/displacement addressing

terms.note: The memory address the instruction really uses.
A register holds the start of the array or structure.
A 16-bit signed constant in the instruction, counted in **bytes**.

steps.why: The base register can point anywhere in memory, while the small offset picks an element near it. That is how one 16-bit field reaches any array.
steps.real: Reading A[i] in C, a field of a struct or a local variable on the stack all compile to a base + offset load.

mistake.right: The offset counts bytes. For an array of words use 4 × index.

notes.explain: Write the formula on the whiteboard and keep it there for the walkthrough.

steps.title: Try it: effective address

blocks.title: lw $t0, offset($s1)

stages.label: Memory
stages.text: The word at that address goes to `$t0`

blocks.hint: Drag the offset to a value that is not a multiple of 4 and watch the alignment stage.

steps.why: Effective address first, memory access second.

steps.question: Array A of words starts at `0x10010000`. What is the address of `A[5]`?
steps.result: Each word is 4 bytes, so A[5] is 20 bytes past the start.

steps.title: Run it: two loads, an add and a store

blocks.title: Using A[1] and A[3]
blocks.hint: $s1 = 0x10010000 is the base. A[1] = 7 and A[3] = 9. Where is the result stored?

steps.why: Each of the three memory instructions forms its own effective address from $s1.

steps.title: Bytes, halfwords and words

items: Loading a negative byte with the wrong instruction gives the wrong number

steps.why: Text is stored in bytes, so byte loads and stores are everywhere in string-handling code.
steps.real: Reading one character of a string is a byte load.

steps.title: Run it: lb versus lbu

blocks.title: Same byte, two instructions
blocks.hint: The word holds 128 = 0x80 in its last byte.

steps.why: The byte 0x80 is −128 as a signed value and 128 as an unsigned one.

steps.question: `$s1 = 0x1000`. What address does `lw $t0, -4($s1)` read?
feedback: That adds 4 instead of subtracting it.
Only one byte below; a word offset is 4 bytes.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. The offset in `lw` is a signed 16-bit number of bytes.
2. A[i] for words is at base + 4 × i.
4. The effective address is computed by the ALU.
steps.explain: `lbu` is the unsigned load: it zero-extends. `lb` sign-extends.

questions.q: How is the effective address of lw formed?
questions.a: Base register plus the sign-extended 16-bit byte offset.

steps.title: PC-relative addressing

terms.note: The address of the instruction that runs next if the branch is taken.
The address of the instruction after the branch.
The 16-bit offset counts **instructions** (words), so it is multiplied by 4.

steps.why: Branch targets are usually close, so a small signed offset is enough, and the code works wherever it is loaded in memory.
steps.real: Every if, while and for loop compiles to branches like this.

mistake.wrong: The branch offset counts bytes from the branch itself.
mistake.right: It counts instructions from the instruction **after** the branch (PC + 4).

explainAgain.beginner: "Skip the next 3 instructions" is the same wherever the code sits.

steps.title: Try it: branch and jump targets
steps.why: A branch reaches nearby code; a jump reaches anywhere in the same 256 MB region.

steps.question: A `beq` is at address `0x00400010` and its offset field is 3. If the branch is taken, what is the target?
steps.result: Count from the instruction after the branch.

steps.title: See the offset in the encoding

blocks.title: A branch in machine code
blocks.hint: The branch field holds the offset in instructions. The jump holds the address shifted right by 2.

steps.why: The offset 3 is stored as the 16-bit value 0x0003; the hardware multiplies by 4 and adds it to PC + 4.

steps.question: In `li $t0,0 / li $t1,5 / loop: addi $t0,$t0,1 / slt $t2,$t0,$t1 / bne $t2,$zero,loop` the code starts at 0x00400000. What is the branch offset field of `bne`?
feedback: That counts from the branch itself rather than the next instruction.
The target is behind the branch, so the offset is negative.
−12 is in bytes; the field counts instructions.

steps.statement: A `j` instruction forms its target with PC-relative addressing.
steps.why: `j` uses pseudo-direct addressing: the 26-bit field times 4, joined with the top bits of PC + 4.

steps.title: Jumps: pseudo-direct addressing

items: Target = (top 4 bits of PC + 4) followed by (26-bit field × 4)
Reaches any instruction in the same 256 MB region
`jr $ra` jumps to an address held in a register, so it can reach anywhere

steps.why: A jump needs more reach than a branch, so it gets almost the whole instruction word.

steps.title: Alignment

items: A word must start at an address that is a **multiple of 4**
A halfword at a multiple of 2; a byte anywhere
Then one memory access fetches a whole word
A misaligned `lw` makes the MIPS machine fault

steps.why: Aligned data lets hardware read a word in one step instead of two, so alignment rules keep memory fast and simple.
steps.real: Compilers pad structures so that each field is aligned.

mistake.right: `lw` needs an address that is a multiple of 4.

steps.question: `$s1 = 0x10010000`. What happens when `lw $t0, 2($s1)` runs?
options: The processor reports an alignment error

reveal.text: 0x10010002 is not a multiple of 4, so the load faults.

steps.result: Run the next demo to see the simulator report it.

steps.title: Run it: a misaligned load

blocks.title: Misaligned word load
blocks.hint: Change the offset from 2 to 0 or 4 and run again.

steps.why: Offsets 0, 4, 8 and so on keep the address a multiple of 4.

steps.title: Big endian and little endian
steps.why: A 32-bit word occupies four bytes, and the machine must decide which byte goes at the lowest address.
steps.real: x86 and most modern chips are little endian; network protocols use big endian ("network byte order"). MIPS can be either.

mistake.wrong: Endianness changes the value of a word.
mistake.right: It changes only the order of the bytes in memory, not the value in a register.

steps.title: Run it: which byte is first?

blocks.title: Big endian (the default here)
blocks.hint: $t0 = 0x01020304. $t1 is the byte at the lowest address; $t2 is the byte at the highest.

steps.why: The register $t0 is identical; only the bytes you read back differ.

steps.question: On a **little-endian** machine the word 0x01020304 is stored at address 0x1000. Which byte is at address 0x1000?

reveal.text: Little endian puts the **least significant** byte first: 0x04 at 0x1000.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Two computers of different byte order exchange a binary file of 32-bit numbers. What goes wrong, and how do real systems avoid it?
steps.answer: Each 32-bit number is read with its bytes in the wrong order, so 0x01020304 becomes 0x04030201. Systems agree a byte order (for example network byte order, which is big endian) and convert at the edges.

notes.explain: Connect to file formats and network protocols.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Should hardware allow misaligned loads and stores?
ideas: Allowing them makes simple programs easier to write.
But the hardware may need two memory accesses, which is slower and more complex.
Many RISC designs forbid them to keep memory access simple and fast.
Some CPUs allow them but run them more slowly.

steps.question: Name the five MIPS addressing modes.
steps.answer: Immediate, register, base/displacement, PC-relative and pseudo-direct.
steps.solution: The first two give operands; base/displacement forms a data address; PC-relative and pseudo-direct form branch and jump targets.

steps.question: `$s1 = 0x10010000`. Give the effective address of `lw $t0, 24($s1)` and of A[7] in an array of words starting at $s1.
steps.hint: Convert the decimal offset to hex before adding.
steps.mistake: Adding 24 to the address in decimal and leaving it unconverted.

steps.question: A `beq` is at 0x00400100 and its offset field is −6. What is the target if taken?
steps.mistake: Starting from the branch address instead of PC + 4.

steps.question: Is `lw $t0, 10($s1)` valid when `$s1 = 0x10010000`? Give the address and your reason.
steps.answer: No. The address is 0x1001000A, which is not a multiple of 4, so the load is misaligned.
steps.solution: 0x10010000 + 10 = 0x1001000A. 10 mod 4 = 2, so the address is not word-aligned.

steps.question: A program stores records of 12 bytes each, starting at 0x10010000. What is the address of the field at offset 8 inside record number 5 (counting from record 0)?
steps.solution: Record 5 starts at 5 × 12 = 60 bytes from the base. Add the field offset 8: 68 = 0x44, giving 0x10010044.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: A word 0x0A0B0C0D is stored at address 0x2000. Which byte is at 0x2001 on a big-endian and on a little-endian machine?
steps.solution: Big endian stores 0A 0B 0C 0D at 0x2000 to 0x2003, so 0x2001 holds 0B. Little endian stores 0D 0C 0B 0A, so 0x2001 holds 0C.
steps.mistake: Reading the bytes in the same order on both machines.
steps.title: Exam practice: byte order

steps.question: A `j` at 0x00400000 jumps to the label at 0x00400040. What 26-bit field is stored, and what target does the hardware compute?
steps.answer: The field is 0x100010; the target is 0x00400040.
steps.solution: 0x00400040 ÷ 4 = 0x100010 (a shift right by 2). The hardware computes (PC + 4)[31:28] with 0x100010 × 4 = 0x00400040.
steps.mistake: Storing the byte address 0x00400040 without shifting.
steps.title: Exam practice: jump target

steps.question: Explain why a branch offset is relative to the PC and counted in instructions.
steps.answer: Targets are usually close, so a short signed offset is enough, and relative offsets keep code position-independent. Counting in instructions makes a 16-bit field reach four times further, since every instruction is 4 bytes.
steps.solution: A strong answer mentions short distances, relocation, and the factor of 4.

steps.title: What you should remember
remember: Addressing modes: immediate, register, base/displacement, PC-relative, pseudo-direct.
Effective address of lw/sw = base register + sign-extended byte offset.
A word array element i is at base + 4 × i.
Jump target joins the top 4 bits of PC + 4 with the 26-bit field × 4.
Words must be aligned to multiples of 4; byte order may be big or little endian.

mistakes.wrong: A branch offset is measured from the branch itself.
mistakes.right: It is measured from PC + 4, in instructions.
It changes only byte order in memory.

mistakes.wrong: Any address is valid for lw.
mistakes.right: Word addresses must be multiples of 4.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Operands and targets are found with a few addressing modes. Loads and stores add a byte offset to a base register; branches add an instruction offset to PC + 4; jumps join a 26-bit field with the PC. Words must be aligned, and a machine may store the bytes of a word in big or little endian order.

questions.question: Which mode is used by `addi $t0, $s1, 4`?
questions.why: The constant 4 is inside the instruction.
questions.misconception: Branch and jump instructions use PC-relative and pseudo-direct modes.

questions.statement: A word load needs an address that is a multiple of 4.
questions.why: Aligned words can be read in a single memory access.
questions.misconception: Misaligned word accesses fault on MIPS.

questions.question: In `lw $t0, 8($s1)`, how is the address formed?
questions.misconception: The offset is already in bytes; do not multiply it.

questions.question: A taken `beq` at 0x00400020 has offset 5. What is the target?
questions.misconception: Start from PC + 4 and multiply the offset by 4.

questions.question: On a little-endian machine, which byte of 0xAABBCCDD is stored at the lowest address?
questions.why: The least significant byte comes first.
questions.misconception: 0xAA is first on a big-endian machine.

questions.question: An array of words starts at 0x10010000. What is the address of A[9]?
questions.misconception: Multiply the index by 4, then convert to hex.

questions.question: A `beq` at 0x00400040 branches back to 0x00400030. What is its offset field?
questions.misconception: Count from PC + 4 and divide the byte distance by 4.

questions.question: Which of these loads is valid for a word when $s1 = 0x10010000?
questions.why: 12 is a multiple of 4; the others are not.
questions.misconception: The effective address must be a multiple of 4.
